html:
French Equatorial Africa was a federation of four French colonies in Central Africa, from 1910 to 1958, run from Brazzaville. The map shows it from 1914 to 1938. Its members were:

  • Gabon;
  • Middle Congo, today's Republic of the Congo;
  • Ubangi-Shari, today's Central African Republic;
  • Chad, a separate colony from 1920.

It was the poorer partner of French West Africa. France handed much of the land to private concession companies, which forced people to gather rubber and ivory, and abuses were widespread. Building the Congo-Ocean railway from Brazzaville to the sea, from 1921 to 1934, cost the lives of many thousands of forced labourers.

In the Second World War the federation mattered more than ever. In August 1940 the governor of Chad, Félix Éboué, the first Black governor of a French colony, rallied it to Charles de Gaulle, and the rest of the federation followed. Brazzaville became the capital of Free France in Africa, and in 1944 de Gaulle held a conference there on the future of the colonies. The federation was dissolved in 1958, and its four members became independent in 1960.
